vignette:
At 30, she has already lived several distinct lives. She grows up in Oceania in a family that values usefulness, steadiness, and getting on with what needs to be done. By the time she is in her twenties, those qualities have become central to how she sees herself. She is practical, capable, and drawn to work that puts her close to people in crisis. Before becoming a parole officer, she spends time overseas as a relief worker in a war zone, telling herself that if she can be helpful in even a small way, then the danger around her will be worth bearing.

At first, she experiences the work as intense but meaningful. She helps distribute supplies, coordinates transport, and spends long days moving between damaged neighborhoods where families gather what is left of their lives. She learns to keep her face calm when others are panicking. She sleeps lightly, eats when she can, and tells jokes with coworkers in the evenings because it is easier than letting herself feel the weight of what she sees. She writes short messages home that make things sound manageable.

The event she returns to most often happens on an ordinary workday, which is part of what makes it feel so treacherous now. Her team is moving aid through an area they have traveled before. There is no warning she can make sense of afterward—just a sudden blast, dust, screaming, and then the stunned, unreal silence that follows when the mind cannot catch up. She remembers the smell first, then fragments: shattered concrete, someone calling for help, blood on clothing that is not hers and then is, in a way, because she is kneeling in it. She tries to help the wounded while scanning for another attack. One of the local staff members she knows well is badly injured. She can still remember his face turning toward her, as if expecting that she will know what to do. She does what she can with trembling hands, but he dies before they can get him out.

In the days after, she keeps working. She tells herself there is no room to fall apart. Others have lost more. The living still need food, transport, medications, names recorded, bodies identified. She becomes even more efficient, almost stripped down to function. Inside, however, something has shifted. Loud noises make her whole body jolt. She starts noticing exits everywhere she goes. She cannot stand with her back to a door. Sleep becomes thin and unreliable; when she does drift off, she wakes with her heart racing, convinced for a moment that she is back there in the dust and confusion. She begins avoiding certain roads, certain smells, certain songs that were playing in the compound around that time.

When she eventually returns home, people expect relief, gratitude, maybe pride. Instead she feels detached, as if the world around her is too soft and too casual. In supermarkets, the abundance unsettles her. At barbecues, she finds herself staring at the ordinary happiness of others and feeling not envy exactly, but distance. Her marriage, already under strain from long absences and the emotional cost of her work, deteriorates further. Her partner wants her to talk; she cannot find language that does not either flatten what happened or unleash more than either of them can hold. He complains that she is irritable, unreachable, always scanning, never really present. She hears criticism and responds with anger, then shame. Their divorce follows, and although she can list practical reasons for it, she carries a private conviction that the war came home inside her and ruined whatever was left.

She later becomes a parole officer, a role that suits the part of her that values structure, vigilance, and reading danger quickly. She is good at it. She knows how to assess risk, how to keep boundaries clear, how to stay composed with clients who are volatile, manipulative, or frightened. Colleagues describe her as calm under pressure. What they do not see is how much energy it takes. If a client raises his voice unexpectedly, she feels a surge of heat and adrenaline before her mind can catch up. On prison visits, the clang of doors and the echoing corridors can pull her abruptly into the old bodily certainty that something terrible is about to happen. She never fully relaxes in her office; she positions her chair so she can see the entrance.

Her days are organized and functional, but her nights are another matter. She delays sleep by scrolling on her phone or cleaning the kitchen because sleep is where the memories ambush her. Sometimes she dreams of the explosion in exact sensory fragments. Other times the dreams are less literal but carry the same helplessness—trying to reach someone she cannot save, trying to shout over noise that swallows her voice. She wakes sweating, disoriented, and then feels foolish in the morning for being shaken by something years in the past.

She avoids news from conflict zones, though she also feels compelled to check it. She has become wary of closeness. Dating feels exhausting and faintly dangerous, not because she expects direct harm, but because intimacy might require her to stop managing herself so tightly. She tells friends she is busy, which is often true, but the fuller truth is that being alone feels easier than explaining why she startles, why crowded places wear her out, why some part of her is always braced.

What troubles her most is not only fear, but the change in her sense of self. She used to believe that competence could protect her, or at least redeem exposure to danger. Now she lives with the persistent feeling that catastrophe can enter without warning and that the people who survive are left carrying impossible images. She continues showing up to work, writing reports, meeting clients, answering calls, and appearing solid. Beneath that surface, she is still measuring threat, still bargaining with memory, still living as though the next blast may already be on its way.
